textbook_segments.title: Tally Marks on Bones and Other Surfaces

textbook_items_in_class.description: Without using Hindu number names or numerals, devise methods for +, –, ×, ÷ using the stick-based number system (Method 1). (Math Talk)
Extend the letter-sound number system (Method 2) beyond 26 using multi-letter strings so that all numbers can be represented; propose and describe the extension scheme. (Math Talk)

time_bands.activity: Open with the question: what would life look like if we could not count? Students share ideas about trade, farming, and tracking time. The teacher draws out examples from the chapter's framing — Stone Age needs for counting food, animals, and celestial events — using the chapter's prose as a prompt rather than copying it.

The class examines the idea of body parts as a counting system, drawing on the Papua New Guinea example of 27 body-part locations used as a standard counting sequence. Students map the sequence on a quick sketch, discuss what this reveals about the earliest 'number systems', and note what operations would be difficult or impossible with this method.

The teacher introduces the Lebombo bone and Ishango bone as evidence of tally-mark counting — two of the oldest known number representations. Students discuss: what mathematical need do notches answer? What can they represent, and what can they not?

Pair work on Figure it Out Q1, p.54 ("Without using Hindu number names or numerals, devise methods for +, –, ×, ÷ using the stick-based number system….") and Figure it Out Q2, p.54 ("Extend the letter-sound number system (Method 2) beyond 26 using multi-letter strings…."). Pairs share one method each; class notes what makes a notation practical.

periods.teacher_notes: The Yajurveda Samhita naming numbers as powers of ten, and the Bakhshali manuscript as the earliest known written use of ten digits including zero, give students a concrete anchor for why the chapter's history matters. Watch for students who assume tally marks are 'too primitive to be a number system' — the bones show deliberate grouping and are a genuine system. Figure it Out Q3, p.54 ("Invent your own number system") makes a productive self-study extension.
materials: Plain paper and pencils for sketching body-part map

textbook_segments.title: Number Names Obtained by Counting in Twos

periods.activity_title: Counting in Groups: Twos to Roman Landmarks

textbook_items_in_class.description: Two inline prompts: (a) identify how Gumulgal names for 3, 4, 5, 6 are formed by counting in 2s; (b) compare the Gumulgal, Bakairi, and Bushmen systems and discuss the possible common-ancestor theory.
Represent the following numbers in the Roman system: (i) 1222, (ii) 2999, (iii) 302, (iv) 715.
Representing 27 in Roman numerals: 27 = 10+10+5+1+1, so XXVII.

time_bands.activity: The teacher presents the Gumulgal (Australia), Bakairi (South America), and Bushmen (South Africa) systems from section 3.2.III. Students work through Math Talk, p.56 ("Two inline prompts: (a) identify how Gumulgal names for 3, 4, 5, 6 are formed by counting in 2s; (b) compare the Gumulgal, Bakairi, and Bushmen systems….") in small groups, listing how compound names are built.

Class discussion: what does counting in twos reveal about the idea of a 'group size'? Students are guided to generalise that 2, 5, 10, and 20 can all serve as organising units, and that the human perceptual limit of recognising fewer than five objects at a glance motivates grouping.

The teacher walks through Example, p.58 ("Representing 27 in Roman numerals: 27 = 10+10+5+1+1, so XXVII.") as a model, then shows Example, p.59 for 2367. Students observe that Roman landmarks (I, V, X, L, C, D, M) are not powers of a fixed base, and discuss what that implies for large-number arithmetic.

Students independently attempt Figure it Out Q1, p.59 ("Represent the following numbers in the Roman system: (i) 1222, (ii) 2999, (iii) 302, (iv) 715."). The teacher circulates, prompting students to check their grouping order from largest landmark to smallest.

periods.teacher_notes: Building on the idea that tally marks count one at a time, this unit shows how grouping — first in twos, then in Roman landmark clusters — reduces the number of symbols needed. A common error is writing Roman subtractive forms (e.g., IX for 9) before the chapter introduces that convention; the textbook's approach groups addictively from largest to smallest, so redirect students who subtract. Example (addition), p.59 ("Adding CCXXXII + CCCCXIII in Roman numerals….") is a good self-study item for students who finish early.

periods.activity_title: Roman and Egyptian Systems in Action

textbook_items_in_class.description: Find the products of Roman landmark number pairs without converting to Hindu numerals: V×L, L×D, V×D, VII×IX.
Identify features of the Hindu number system that make it more efficient than the Roman number system. (Math Talk)
Represent the following numbers in the Egyptian hieroglyphic system: 10458, 1023, 2660, 784, 1111, 70707.
Representing 324 in Egyptian hieroglyphic numerals: 324 = 100+100+100+10+10+4, written with three 100-symbols, two 10-symbols, four 1-symbols.

homework.description: Decode two given Egyptian numerals (i) and (ii) and state the numbers they represent.

time_bands.activity: Students attempt Try This, p.60 ("Find the products of Roman landmark number pairs without converting to Hindu numerals: V×L, L×D, V×D, VII×IX.") in pairs. After attempting, they compare answers and discuss: why is Roman multiplication cumbersome? What structural property of the landmarks makes it hard?

Class discussion using Figure it Out Q3, p.61 ("Identify features of the Hindu number system that make it more efficient than the Roman number system.") as a prompt. Students articulate at least two structural reasons; the teacher records these on the board as a comparative table.

The teacher introduces the Egyptian number system: each power of 10 up to 10⁷ has a distinct hieroglyphic symbol. Example, p.62 ("Representing 324 in Egyptian hieroglyphic numerals: 324 = 100+100+100+10+10+4….") is walked through together, connecting the grouping idea to powers of 10.

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, p.62 ("Represent the following numbers in the Egyptian hieroglyphic system: 10458, 1023, 2660, 784, 1111, 70707."). The teacher encourages students to check their work by reversing the encoding.

periods.teacher_notes: The key insight connecting the Roman and Egyptian sections is that Egyptian landmarks are successive powers of 10, which gives the system a regularity Roman numerals lack. Watch for students who use more than nine of any symbol in Egyptian notation — the rule that ten of any symbol regroup into the next higher symbol should be drawn out from the structure, not stated as a rule to memorise. Figure it Out Q2, p.62 ("Decode two given Egyptian numerals….") is assigned as homework to reinforce both directions of encoding.
materials: Reference sketches of Egyptian hieroglyphic symbols (drawn on board)

textbook_segments.title: Variations on the Egyptian System and the Notion of Base

periods.activity_title: Bases, Arithmetic, and Why Egyptian Falls Short

textbook_items_in_class.description: Is there any number that cannot be represented in the base-5 system constructed in the section? Explain why or why not.
Compute the landmark numbers of a base-7 system. In general, state what the landmark numbers of a base-n system are.
Can any Egyptian numeral have a symbol occurring 10 or more times? Explain why not. (Math Talk)
Expressing 143 in the constructed base-5 system: 143 = 125+5+5+5+1+1+1, written using base-5 symbols for 125, three 5s, three 1s.
Multiplying a compound Egyptian numeral by 10 using the distributive property: (100 + 10 + 1) × 10 = 1000 + 100 + 10, each landmark number moving up one power.

homework.description: Create your own base-4 number system and represent all numbers from 1 to 16 in it. (Math Talk)

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the base-5 system from section 3.3.II, using Example, p.63 ("Expressing 143 in the constructed base-5 system: 143 = 125+5+5+5+1+1+1….") to model how any integer n ≥ 2 can serve as a base with landmark numbers being powers of n. Students confirm the decomposition and try a second number of their own choice.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, p.63 ("Is there any number that cannot be represented in the base-5 system….") and Figure it Out Q3, p.63 ("Compute the landmark numbers of a base-7 system. In general, state what the landmark numbers of a base-n system are."). The teacher brings the class together to articulate the general rule: landmark numbers of a base-n system are 1, n, n², n³, …

The teacher demonstrates multiplication in the Egyptian system using Example (multiplication), p.67 ("Multiplying a compound Egyptian numeral by 10 using the distributive property: (100 + 10 + 1) × 10 = 1000 + 100 + 10…."). Students see that the distributive law operates cleanly when landmark numbers are powers of a fixed base.

The class reasons through Figure it Out Q1, p.69 ("Can any Egyptian numeral have a symbol occurring 10 or more times? Explain why not.") as a whole-class deductive argument, then the teacher articulates the fundamental shortcoming of section 3.3.III: arbitrarily large numbers require new symbols, so the system cannot represent all numbers with a finite symbol set.

periods.teacher_notes: The move from Egyptian to a general base-n framework is the conceptual pivot of the chapter — students should see that choosing powers of a fixed base as landmarks is what makes multiplication by the base trivially systematic. A frequent confusion is treating 'base-5' as meaning 'count to 5 then restart', conflating a positional system with a grouping system; the distinction becomes clear when students write out landmark numbers explicitly. Figure it Out Q2, p.70 ("Create your own base-4 number system….") is assigned as homework to consolidate the general principle before place value is introduced.

periods.activity_title: Place Value, Zero, and the Hindu Culmination

textbook_items_in_class.description: Represent the following numbers in the Mesopotamian (base-60 positional) system: (i) 63, (ii) 132, (iii) 200, (iv) 60, (v) 3605.
Represent the following numbers using the Mayan system: (i) 77, (ii) 100, (iii) 361, (iv) 721.
Form a base-2 place value system using 'ukasar' (=1) and 'urapon' (=0) as digits; compare this with the Gumulgal counting-by-2s system.
Representing 640 and 7530 in the Mesopotamian system: 640 = 10×60+40 written as two positional groups; 7530 = 2×3600+5×60+30 written as three positional groups.

homework.description: If humans had only 8 fingers, what base would we likely use? Write the base-10 numeral 25 in base-8, base-5, and base-2. (Math Talk)

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces Mesopotamian base-60 place value using Example, p.71–72 ("Representing 640 and 7530 in the Mesopotamian system: 640 = 10×60+40…."). Students see that dropping the landmark-number labels and relying on position allows a finite symbol set to represent all numbers, and they discuss the problem of blank spaces — ambiguity without a zero placeholder.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, p.73 ("Represent the following numbers in the Mesopotamian (base-60 positional) system: (i) 63, (ii) 132, (iii) 200, (iv) 60, (v) 3605.") in pairs. The teacher highlights cases where a zero placeholder is needed to avoid ambiguity.

The class surveys the Mayan system via section 3.4.II — dot for 1, bar for 5, seashell for zero — and students work the Inline prompt, p.76 ("Represent the following numbers using the Mayan system: (i) 77, (ii) 100, (iii) 361, (iv) 721."). The teacher draws out the near-base-20 structure and the calendar-driven irregularity at the third position.

The Chinese rod numeral system is introduced briefly (section 3.4.III) — alternating Zong and Heng symbols distinguish adjacent place values. The unit closes with section 3.4.IV: students reason through Figure it Out Q2, p.80 ("Form a base-2 place value system using 'ukasar' (=1) and 'urapon' (=0) as digits; compare this with the Gumulgal counting-by-2s system."), bringing together the ideas of base, position, and zero as distinct features whose union defines the Hindu system.

periods.teacher_notes: The reasoning arc here builds from the shortcoming of the Egyptian system — needing new symbols for every new power — to the Mesopotamian insight that position alone can encode a power, and finally to the Hindu system where zero is a full number, not merely a placeholder. A common confusion is equating a zero-placeholder with zero-as-number; Brahmagupta's codification of arithmetic on zero and negative numbers (628 CE) is the precise moment the distinction becomes operational. Figure it Out Q4, p.80 ("If humans had only 8 fingers, what base would we likely use?") is assigned as homework to extend the reasoning about base choice.
materials: Reference sketch of Mayan symbols (dot, bar, seashell) drawn on board

textbook_segments.title: Number Names Obtained by Counting in Twos
Variations on the Egyptian System and the Notion of Base

periods.teacher_notes: Refer to Prepared Table (see material: 'Problems and solutions') for the problems in full and their worked solutions. Pose all four problems at once on the board. Students work individually for the first stretch, writing full working. They then compare in groups of three: any disagreement is reconstructed step by step before the group agrees on an answer. One student per problem presents to the class; after each presentation the class names the chapter method the solution rested on — do not name it yourself first. Problem 1 needs Roman numeral grouping into landmark numbers (largest to smallest). Problem 2 needs Egyptian hieroglyphic encoding and the base-10 regrouping rule for addition. Problem 3 needs the greedy decomposition into powers of a base (base-5 here). Problem 4 needs the positional (place value) reading of a Mesopotamian-style numeral. Watch for students who add Roman symbols without checking landmark order, who forget to regroup ten strokes into one arc in the Egyptian sum, who treat 5¹ and 5⁰ as interchangeable in the base-5 decomposition, and who assign face value rather than positional value to the Mesopotamian groups.

visual_aids.title: Problems and solutions
visual_aids.table:
No. | Problem | Solution
1 | Write 2468 in Roman numerals. Show your grouping step by step. | 2468 = 1000+1000+100+100+100+100+50+10+5+1+1+1. Group from largest landmark: MM (2000) + CCCC (400) + L (50) + X (10) + V (5) + III (3) = MMCCCCLXVIII.
2 | Add these two Egyptian hieroglyphic numbers: one has 3 hundred-symbols, 7 ten-symbols and 6 one-symbols; the other has 2 hundred-symbols, 5 ten-symbols and 8 one-symbols. Write the sum in Egyptian notation. | Ones: 6+8=14 → keep 4 ones, carry 1 ten. Tens: 7+5+1=13 → keep 3 tens, carry 1 hundred. Hundreds: 3+2+1=6 hundreds. Sum: 6 hundred-symbols, 3 ten-symbols, 4 one-symbols (representing 634).
3 | Express 97 in a base-5 system whose landmark numbers are 1, 5, 25, 125. Show the greedy decomposition. | 97 ÷ 25 = 3 remainder 22. 22 ÷ 5 = 4 remainder 2. 2 ÷ 1 = 2. So 97 = 3×25 + 4×5 + 2×1. Written with base-5 symbols: three 25-symbols, four 5-symbols, two 1-symbols (digit form: 342 in base 5).
4 | A Mesopotamian scribe writes a numeral in two positional groups: the left group shows 2×10+15 = 35, and the right group shows 1×10+10 = 20. The left group stands in the 60¹ place and the right in the 60⁰ place. What number is this? | Left group value: 35 × 60 = 2100. Right group value: 20 × 1 = 20. Total: 2100 + 20 = 2120.

time_bands.activity: Write all four problems on the board without comment. Tell the class: work each one fully, showing every step. Silence while everyone reads and begins.

Individual working time. Students write complete solutions to all four problems on rough paper. No answers shared yet. Move around the room; if a student is stuck on a problem, ask which chapter system the problem is asking them to use — nothing more.
Groups of three compare answers. Where answers differ, the group works through the disagreement step by step on paper until they agree. Every member must be able to explain the agreed solution.

One student presents each problem's solution at the board, talking through every step. After each presentation, the class names the chapter method the solution used. The teacher writes the method name on the board beside the problem number once the class has named it.

The teacher reads the four method names now on the board and speaks one sentence: every number system in this chapter was an attempt to answer the same question — how do you write any number clearly, with as few symbols as possible, so that arithmetic stays manageable — and the Hindu system answered it completely because it brought all five ideas together at once.

items.prompt: Which of the following correctly identifies the document that contains the earliest known written use of all ten digits including zero?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The Bakhshali manuscript (approximately 3rd century CE) contains the earliest known written use of all ten digits including zero.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall the chapter's account of the origin of the modern number system in ancient India.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confuses the Yajurveda Samhita — which named numbers as powers of ten but did not use a written zero digit — with the first ten-digit written record.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student recalls Aryabhata's systematisation of the Indian number system (499 CE) but conflates systematisation with the earliest written use of all ten digits.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student recalls Al-Khwarizmi's role in transmitting Hindu numerals to the Arab world but confuses transmission with origin.

inclusivity.support: Reread the opening paragraph of the chapter, which names each document and its date.
inclusivity.challenge: Name one additional historical figure from the chapter who helped transmit this system westward, and state what role they played.

exercise.description: Without using Hindu number names or numerals, devise methods for +, –, ×, ÷ using the stick-based number system (Method 1). (Math Talk)

items.section_title: Number Names Obtained by Counting in Twos
items.prompt: In the Gumulgal counting system, numbers are built by combining two base words: 'ukasar' (meaning 1) and 'ukasar-ukasar' (meaning 2). What is the Gumulgal name for the number 4?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 4 in Gumulgal is formed as two groups of two: ukasar-ukasar (2) repeated twice, giving ukasar-ukasar-ukasar-ukasar. The system counts in twos, so 4 = 2 + 2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Recall that Gumulgal names are built by compounding groups of two, so 4 = 2 + 2 = ukasar-ukasar + ukasar-ukasar.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student counts three repetitions of ukasar, treating the system as a simple tally rather than a grouping-in-twos system.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student correctly assembles four ukasar tokens but does not yet connect this to the two-group structure the chapter describes.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student introduces 'urapon' (zero/none) from the binary context, misapplying a later concept to the Gumulgal system.

inclusivity.support: Reread the Gumulgal table in section 3.2.III and trace how 3 and 5 are formed before attempting 4.
inclusivity.challenge: Using the same compounding rule, write the Gumulgal name for 6 and explain why the name has the structure it does.

exercise.description: Two inline prompts: (a) identify how Gumulgal names for 3, 4, 5, 6 are formed by counting in 2s; (b) compare the Gumulgal, Bakairi, and Bushmen systems and discuss the possible common-ancestor theory.

items.section_title: Variations on the Egyptian System and the Notion of Base
items.prompt: A student claims: 'In a base-5 number system, the number 37 cannot be represented because 37 is not a power of 5 or a sum of powers of 5.' Is the student correct? Explain your reasoning using the structure of a base-n system.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The student is incorrect. In a base-5 system, the landmark numbers are 1, 5, 25, 125, … and any positive integer can be decomposed into a sum of these landmarks (with each landmark used at most four times, since five of any landmark regroup into the next). 37 = 25 + 5 + 5 + 1 + 1 = 25 + 10 + 2, i.e., one 25, two 5s, and two 1s. Because the decomposition algorithm always terminates — at each step we subtract the largest landmark that fits — every positive integer is representable.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply the landmark-decomposition algorithm: repeatedly subtract the largest power of 5 that fits, stopping when the remainder is zero.

inclusivity.support: Try decomposing 37 step by step: what is the largest power of 5 that is ≤ 37? Subtract it and repeat until nothing remains.
inclusivity.challenge: Change the base to 7 and show that 100 can be represented; then state a general argument for why every positive integer is representable in any base-n system.

exercise.description: Is there any number that cannot be represented in the base-5 system constructed in the section? Explain why or why not.

items.prompt: The Mesopotamian number system used base 60 and relied on position to indicate which power of 60 a group of symbols represented. Explain why blank spaces in a Mesopotamian numeral caused ambiguity, and describe the solution the later Mesopotamians introduced to address this problem. What limitation did this solution still have?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: In a positional system, the value of a symbol group depends on which position (column) it occupies. If a power of 60 is absent — for example, there are no units in the 60s place — the scribe left a blank space. But a blank space could be misread as no gap at all, making 'two groups with a gap' look like 'two adjacent groups', changing the number's value entirely. The later Mesopotamians introduced a special placeholder symbol written in medial positions to mark absent powers explicitly. The remaining limitation was that this placeholder was not used at the end of a numeral, so trailing absent powers (analogous to trailing zeros today) still caused ambiguity.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reason from the definition of a positional system: value depends on position, so a missing position must be marked unambiguously, and a gap symbol serves this purpose in medial but not terminal positions.

inclusivity.support: Think about how 'two groups next to each other' could look the same as 'two groups with something missing between them', then read section 3.4.I's description of the placeholder symbol.
inclusivity.challenge: Compare the Mesopotamian placeholder with the Mayan seashell zero: in what way does the Mayan zero go further, and in what way does it still fall short of the Hindu zero?

exercise.description: Represent the following numbers in the Mesopotamian (base-60 positional) system: (i) 63, (ii) 132, (iii) 200, (iv) 60, (v) 3605.

items.prompt: Write the Roman numeral for 1764. Then write the Roman numeral for 2436. Finally, add these two Roman numerals by combining and regrouping their symbols — without converting to Hindu numerals — and state the result as a Roman numeral.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 1764 in Roman numerals: 1000 + 500 + 100 + 100 + 50 + 10 + 4 = MDCCLXIV. 2436 in Roman numerals: 1000 + 1000 + 400 + 30 + 6 = MMCDXXXVI. Adding: M+MM = MMM; DCC + CD = MCCC (since D + C = DC, and DC + CD = M + 300 — more carefully: 1764 + 2436 = 4200 = 4000 + 200 = MMMMCC). Verification: 1764 + 2436 = 4200; MMMMCC = 4×1000 + 2×100 = 4200. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose each number into Roman landmark groups, combine symbol counts for each landmark, and regroup where any symbol appears five or more times.

inclusivity.support: Write out each number as a sum of Roman landmark values (1000s first, then 500s, and so on) before assembling the symbols.
inclusivity.challenge: Now compute the difference 2436 − 1764 in Roman numerals by removing matching symbol groups, and state any regrouping steps you needed.

exercise.description: Find the products of Roman landmark number pairs without converting to Hindu numerals: V×L, L×D, V×D, VII×IX.

items.prompt: Represent the number 2305 in the Egyptian hieroglyphic system by writing out its decomposition into powers of 10, stating how many of each hieroglyphic symbol is needed. Then represent 1095 in the same way. Finally, add the two Egyptian numerals together, showing any regrouping step.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2305: 2×1000 + 3×100 + 0×10 + 5×1. In Egyptian hieroglyphics: two 1000-symbols, three 100-symbols, zero 10-symbols, five 1-symbols. 1095: 1×1000 + 0×100 + 9×10 + 5×1. In Egyptian: one 1000-symbol, zero 100-symbols, nine 10-symbols, five 1-symbols. Addition: 1000s: 2+1 = 3 → three 1000-symbols. 100s: 3+0 = 3 → three 100-symbols. 10s: 0+9 = 9 → nine 10-symbols. 1s: 5+5 = 10 → regroup 10 ones into one 10-symbol → 10+1=11 wait: nine 10s + one new 10 = ten 10-symbols → regroup into one 100-symbol. So 10s: 0, 100s: 3+1=4. Final: three 1000-symbols, four 100-symbols, zero 10-symbols, zero 1-symbols = 3400. Verification: 2305 + 1095 = 3400. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose each number into Egyptian landmark groups (powers of 10), combine symbol counts, and regroup whenever ten of any symbol accumulate into one of the next higher symbol.

inclusivity.support: Use a table with columns for 1000, 100, 10, and 1 to tally symbol counts for each number before adding.
inclusivity.challenge: Now subtract 1095 from 2305 in Egyptian notation, showing any ungrouping step where you need to break a higher-value symbol into ten lower-value symbols.

exercise.description: Represent the following numbers in the Egyptian hieroglyphic system: 10458, 1023, 2660, 784, 1111, 70707.

items.prompt: Represent the number 3722 in the Mesopotamian base-60 positional system. Show your decomposition into powers of 60, state the value in each positional group, and write the full positional representation.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Powers of 60: 60² = 3600, 60¹ = 60, 60⁰ = 1. Decompose 3722: 3722 ÷ 3600 = 1 remainder 122. 122 ÷ 60 = 2 remainder 2. 2 ÷ 1 = 2 remainder 0. So 3722 = 1×3600 + 2×60 + 2×1. Positional groups: first position (60²) = 1; second position (60¹) = 2; third position (60⁰) = 2. Verification: 1×3600 + 2×60 + 2 = 3600 + 120 + 2 = 3722. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Divide the number by successive powers of 60, recording the quotient at each positional level as the group value for that power.

inclusivity.support: Start by identifying the largest power of 60 that fits into 3722 (that is 3600 = 60²), then find how many times it fits, and work down from there.
inclusivity.challenge: Now represent 7325 in the Mesopotamian system and identify which positional group would need a placeholder symbol if the system were written left-to-right with no blank spaces.

exercise.description: Why did the Chinese alternate Zong and Heng symbols? How would 41 look using only Zong symbols, and could it be interpreted in multiple ways? (Math Talk)
